children.electedBy: Designated from among the Diet's members by a resolution of the Diet, then appointed by the Emperor. If the two houses disagree, the House of Representatives' choice prevails (Articles 6 and 67).
children.reportsTo: The Diet, and above all the House of Representatives: the Cabinet must resign en masse if that house passes a no-confidence resolution, unless it is dissolved within ten days (Article 69).
children.plain: The head of government. Heads the Cabinet, appoints and can dismiss the other Ministers of State (most of whom must be Diet members) and directs the government's work. The Prime Minister and all ministers must be civilians (Articles 66 and 68).
plainFacts: No fixed term; the Cabinet resigns en masse after each general election of the House of Representatives and the Diet then designates a Prime Minister again
A Diet resolution; the House of Representatives prevails
A no-confidence vote in the House of Representatives, or resigning
Leads the Cabinet, which holds executive power (Article 65)
terms: Designation
The Diet's vote that chooses the Prime Minister before the Emperor formally appoints them.
Dissolution
Ending the House of Representatives' term early to hold a general election. The Emperor does so on the Cabinet's advice.

children.electedBy: Hereditary. The throne is dynastic and passes according to the Imperial House Law, which the Diet passes (Article 2 of the Constitution).
children.reportsTo: The Emperor's position derives "from the will of the people with whom resides sovereign power" (Article 1). Every act in matters of state needs the advice and approval of the Cabinet (Article 3).
children.plain: The head of state in a purely ceremonial role. The Emperor is "the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people" and has no powers related to government (Articles 1 and 4). On the Cabinet's advice and approval, the Emperor performs formal acts such as appointing the Prime Minister (as designated by the Diet), appointing the Chief Justice (as designated by the Cabinet), promulgating laws and convening the Diet (Articles 6 and 7).
plainFacts: Birth, under the Imperial House Law
Cannot be removed; a Regent acts if the Emperor cannot perform his duties (Article 5)
None in government; ceremonial acts only
terms: Imperial House Law
The law, passed by the Diet, that sets the rules of succession to the throne and the Imperial Household.
Matters of state
The formal ceremonial acts listed in the Constitution, which the Emperor performs on the Cabinet's advice.

children.electedBy: 465 members: 289 elected in single-member constituencies and 176 by proportional representation in regional blocs. The term is four years, unless the House is dissolved earlier (Article 45), which is frequent. A general election must follow within 40 days of a dissolution (Article 54).
children.reportsTo: The voters. The Cabinet answers to it and must resign if it passes a no-confidence resolution (Article 69).
children.plain: The more powerful house of the Diet. Its choice of Prime Minister prevails if the houses disagree (Article 67), and it can pass an ordinary bill over the upper house's objection with a two-thirds majority of members present (Article 59). Only this house can bring down the Cabinet.
terms: Single-member constituency
An area that elects one member, the candidate with the most votes.
Proportional representation
Seats given to parties in regional blocs in proportion to their votes.
Dissolution
Ending the House's term early to call a general election.

root.place: Government and the Diet of Japan
root.summary: A parliamentary constitutional monarchy. The Emperor is a symbol of the State with no powers of government. The Diet, made up of the House of Representatives and the House of Councillors, is the highest organ of state power and chooses the Prime Minister, who leads a Cabinet that answers to it.

root.electedBy: Japan's constitution took effect in 1947. Under it the people hold sovereign power, exercised through the Diet, whose members are elected by voters.
